summary: Extends DHCPv6 Leasequery so a requestor can receive a continuous stream of binding updates from a server rather than only data from before the request. It allows real-time transfer of lease information to external systems.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking the librarian who borrowed each book again and again, you get a message whenever one is checked out.

questions: how to get real-time dhcpv6 binding updates
how does active leasequery differ from bulk leasequery
what port does active leasequery use
how does active leasequery recover missed updates
what does the datamissing status mean
subtitle: A long-lived TCP feed that streams DHCPv6 lease changes to outside systems as they happen.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 Leasequery and Bulk Leasequery only return binding data from before the request arrives, but some external systems need to stay current with a server's lease changes continuously.
tldr.mechanism: A requestor opens a TCP connection to the server on port 547 and sends an ACTIVELEASEQUERY message. The server then streams LEASEQUERY-REPLY and LEASEQUERY-DATA messages as bindings change, and can first catch the requestor up on changes since a given time.
tldr.outcome: External entities can follow binding activity in real or near real time, and can recover after a disconnect without re-reading everything. The stream is not a full history of every state change.

today: RFC 7653 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 5460 (DHCPv6 Bulk Leasequery) by adding new options.

sections.title: Why Active Leasequery
sections.content:
DHCPv6 servers keep authoritative binding information for addresses and delegated prefixes. Some external entities need to keep up with that binding activity, which the RFC calls Active Leasequery. The entity could be a relay agent, or any outside process that needs data from the server's lease state database.

DHCPv6 Bulk Leasequery (RFC 5460) can recover information when such an entity starts up, but it cannot follow changes that happen after the request. Active Leasequery lets an entity that is not directly part of the client-server exchange stay current in real time.

The RFC also updates RFC 5460 by adding new options.
sections.eli5: Asking the server for the list once is like checking the board at school one morning. This RFC is like having the board's updates sent to you all day.

sections.title: How the Protocol Fits Together
sections.content:
Active Leasequery is modelled on Bulk Leasequery. A server that supports it MUST support Bulk Leasequery as well. The requestor opens a TCP connection to the server on DHCPv6 port 547 and needs the server's unicast address by configuration or some other means. No relaying is specified.

The requestor sends one ACTIVELEASEQUERY message. The server answers with LEASEQUERY-REPLY and LEASEQUERY-DATA messages, in the same format as Bulk Leasequery, and keeps sending whenever a binding changes. An Active Leasequery connection never completes by itself, though the server can close it for exceptional reasons.

A typical requestor first uses Bulk Leasequery to fill an empty database, then uses Active Leasequery to keep it current. If it loses the connection, it can reconnect and ask for changes since a given time, and the server tells it when it cannot supply them.
sections.eli5: You call the server once and stay on the line. It reads out each change as it happens, and if you hang up by accident you can call back and say, tell me what I missed.

sections.title: New Messages and Options
sections.content:
Two new message types are defined. ACTIVELEASEQUERY asks for binding activity after the request arrives and MUST carry a transaction-id that is locally unique on its TCP connection. STARTTLS asks to set up TLS and should be sent without options. Messages use the same TCP framing as Bulk Leasequery.

A request that wants every binding update MUST NOT include an OPTION_LQ_QUERY option. A requestor interested in specific bindings MAY include one with a query type from RFC 5007 or RFC 5460.

Three new 32-bit-time options are carried as unsigned integers in network byte order:

  • OPTION_LQ_BASE_TIME (100): the server's current absolute time when it created the message. Other times in the reply are relative to it.
  • OPTION_LQ_START_TIME (101): only bindings changed on or after this time should be returned. Allowed in Active and Bulk requests.
  • OPTION_LQ_END_TIME (102): only bindings changed on or before this time. Allowed in Bulk requests, and MUST NOT be used in an Active request.

An absolute time is a 32-bit unsigned count of seconds since midnight UTC, January 1, 2000, modulo 2^32.
sections.eli5: The new messages are like a button to start the feed and a button to make it private. The new time options are bookmarks that say where you stopped listening.

sections.title: Catching Up After a Disconnect
sections.content:
If a requestor includes OPTION_LQ_START_TIME, the server enters a catch-up phase. It sends information about bindings that changed since that time, possibly in parallel with real-time updates. Typically the start time is the latest base-time the requestor received, which marks the last successful contact.

The requestor can tell the catch-up phase is over when it receives a LEASEQUERY-DATA with status CatchUpComplete. Until then it MUST NOT save base-times for later use, because catch-up data does not arrive in update order. If the connection drops first, it must reuse the base-time from the previous connection.

A server may keep only a limited history. If it cannot cover the requested start time, it replies with status DataMissing and its current time as base-time. The requestor should then issue a Bulk Leasequery with the same start time and an end time equal to that base-time.

The stream is not a complete history. The requestor MUST NOT assume every state change is sent: it can assume at least one message for each binding that changed, carrying the latest state.
sections.eli5: If you were away, the server first reads you the latest news about everything that changed. If it forgot some of it, it tells you, and you ask for the missed part another way.

sections.title: Timeouts and Keepalives
sections.content:
Active Leasequery reuses the port configuration, BULK_LQ_DATA_TIMEOUT and BULK_LQ_MAX_CONNS from RFC 5460, and adds three timers. Implementations may make them configurable, but values smaller than the defaults SHOULD NOT be used.

  • ACTIVE_LQ_RCV_TIMEOUT: 120 seconds. A requestor should end a connection whose replies stay blocked this long.
  • ACTIVE_LQ_SEND_TIMEOUT: 120 seconds. A server should close a connection that stays blocked this long.
  • ACTIVE_LQ_IDLE_TIMEOUT: 60 seconds. An idle server sends an empty LEASEQUERY-DATA this often, and requestors should not retry connections more often than this.
sections.eli5: The server sends a quick "still here" ping when nothing is happening. If nobody answers for too long, either side hangs up.

sections.title: Secure and Insecure Modes
sections.content:
Both sides SHOULD be able to run in insecure or secure mode. In secure mode the requestor sends STARTTLS as the first message. If the server answers with a REPLY with no status code, the requestor starts a TLS handshake and MUST validate the server's certificate. If the server stays silent, closes the connection, or replies with TLSConnectionRefused, the requestor must close the TCP connection.

On the server, Active Leasequery MUST NOT be enabled by default, and insecure mode also needs its own explicit configuration step. In secure mode the server validates the requestor's certificate, and connections MUST be mutually authenticated. The RFC says to follow the recommendations in RFC 7525 when negotiating TLS.

A server without Active Leasequery that receives a request SHOULD answer with status NotSupported and close the connection.
sections.eli5: Before sharing private lists, both sides show ID cards. If either card looks wrong, the call ends. The feed is also switched off until someone turns it on on purpose.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general DHCPv6 threats are in RFC 3315, and the Leasequery recommendations in RFC 5007 apply. Long-lived TCP connections add new risks. Attackers can exhaust the server's connection resources, for example by connecting and then sending invalid, partial or no queries.

Servers SHOULD offer settings that limit where connections may come from, using the certificates presented in TLS, and that cap the number of connections and how long idle ones stay open.

Data obtained through Active Leasequery is exposed to the same abuse as the server's own data, so it SHOULD be protected as strongly and deleted as soon as possible after use. DHCP message authentication MUST NOT be used to secure these messages.
sections.eli5: Because the line stays open, a troublemaker could hog all the phone lines. The server limits who may call and how many, and the people who get the news must guard it carefully.

sections.title: Assigned Codes
sections.content: IANA assigned values in three DHCPv6 registries. The new option codes are 100, 101 and 102. The new status codes are DataMissing (12), CatchUpComplete (13), NotSupported (14) and TLSConnectionRefused (15). The new message types are ACTIVELEASEQUERY (22) and STARTTLS (23).
sections.eli5: Each new message, option and status gets its own official number so everyone uses the same one.

fields.name: base-time
fields.desc: The DHCPv6 server's absolute time when the message was created.

items.label: ACTIVELEASEQUERY
items.desc: Message type: asks for ongoing binding updates.

items.label: STARTTLS
items.desc: Message type: asks to set up TLS.

items.label: OPTION_LQ_BASE_TIME
items.desc: Option: server time when the message was created.

items.label: OPTION_LQ_START_TIME
items.desc: Option: only bindings changed on or after this time.

items.label: OPTION_LQ_END_TIME
items.desc: Option: only bindings changed on or before this time.

items.label: DataMissing
items.desc: Status: server lacks the history needed.

items.label: CatchUpComplete
items.desc: Status: catch-up data has all been sent.

items.label: NotSupported
items.desc: Status: server does not support the request.

items.label: TLSConnectionRefused
items.desc: Status: server will not do TLS.
